exclusions.A: It struck me only later that the two Gates, which shared a post at the foot of the hill, carried the latest dates of all, pencilled the spring before he died and hidden on their backs for decades.
exclusions.B: At a town meeting in April, residents voted to hang whatever could be saved in the town hall.
exclusions.C: When the crews lifted the boards in March, most had rotted through at the edges and split as they came off.
exclusions.D: Elias Marrow painted the signs in his workshop on Tanner Street, black letters on cream boards, and it was his custom to pencil his initials and the date on the back of each.

WV12-P01.4.note: The narrator says a fact about the Gates' dates came to mind only later, so "struck" means "occurred to"; nothing is hit, agreed, halted or crossed out.

exclusions.A: On some evenings I still look up at a corner for the cream board and the black letters, the way you look for a face at the window of a house where someone used to live.
exclusions.B: The few boards that held together sat in storage in the depot shed through the summer, and in August they crumbled as the crew lifted them onto a truck.
exclusions.C: I have walked the old route once since, from Tanner Street down to the Gates.
exclusions.D: Those night walks ended in March, and the boards they were built around are gone.

support: On some evenings I still look up at a corner for the cream board and the black letters, the way you look for a face at the window of a house where someone used to live.
I have walked the old route once since, from Tanner Street down to the Gates.
WV12-P01.5.note: The author longs for the vanished boards, comparing looking for them to looking for a lost person's face, which is wistful rather than admiring of their craft, critical, amused or anxious.

exclusions.A: On still evenings the sound of those two hives carried down into the yard, and I used to lie in the grass beside the shed and listen until the light went.
exclusions.C: I would give a great deal to hear the pitch of that hum again, low and steady, climbing a little on the hottest afternoons.
exclusions.D: It was the first thing I listened for each morning and the last each night.
exclusions.E: She sold it on Saturdays at the Brackwell market and kept the table herself.

WV12-P02.4.note: The "pitch" is of a hum described as low and steady and climbing, so it is a sound's tone, not a throw, resin, slope or market stall.

exclusions.A: When I walk down Tamsin Lane in summer, I still stop at her gate for a moment, listening for a sound that went away to Dunmore long ago.
exclusions.B: When my mother heard about the lessons, she asked her whether I would be in the way.
exclusions.C: I would give a great deal to hear the pitch of that hum again, low and steady, climbing a little on the hottest afternoons.

WV12-P02.5.note: The narrator yearns to hear the long-gone hives again and still pauses at the gate listening, a wistful longing; the only worry in the passage is the mother's, not the narrator's.

exclusions.A: As the sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the bank of windows along the school's west wall goes dark, and the first swifts drop into the chimney.
exclusions.B: Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School.
exclusions.D: Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed.
exclusions.E: The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years.

WV12-P04.4.note: A "bank of windows along the school's west wall" is a row of windows, not supplies, a riverbank, a firm or a tilt.

exclusions.A: The chimney I know is only the stump of the one Reyburn knew, and the evenings when ten thousand swifts poured into it are gone for good.
exclusions.C: The masons relaid the top courses of brick in lime mortar rather than cheap cement and set a smooth stone cap over them, leaving the flue open.
exclusions.D: The shortened flue holds a few hundred birds at most.

support: The chimney I know is only the stump of the one Reyburn knew, and the evenings when ten thousand swifts poured into it are gone for good.
Each September evening the few hundred that remain drop into it within a few minutes, and then the sky over Linden Row is empty long before the old flocks would have finished coming down.
WV12-P04.5.note: The writer dwells on the loss of the full chimney and its vast flocks as gone for good, which reads as sadness; the stump is called sound, ruling out apprehension, and nothing is mocked or condemned.
